articles.title: ICE Admits It Investigated a Critic Based on Constitutionally Protected Speech
articles.content:
Last June, two investigators employed by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) showed up at David Streever's house in Rochester, New York. Streever was not home, so they left him a note.
That note, presented as an official warning from Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), is at the center of a First Amendment lawsuit that Streever filed last month, alleging that ICE agents investigated and threatened him based on his constitutionally protected criticism of their boss. This month, the government responded to Streever's lawsuit, confirming his allegations while attempting to rebut them.
On January 26, two days after DHS agents fatally shot Minneapolis protester Alex Pretti, Streever sent an angry email to Todd Lyons, then the acting ICE director. Streever called Lyons "a monstrous human being," likened him to the genocidal Nazi official Reinhard Heydrich, and predicted that he would be haunted by "shame at your own pathetic weakness" in defending the Pretti shooting "until your last day on Earth."
Streever's evaluation of Lyons was harsh, to say the least. But he did not say anything that could reasonably be construed as a threat of violence.
Brent Goodwin, assistant director for investigations at ICE's Office of Professional Responsibility (OPR), nevertheless claims Streever's email "had potential threatening undertones" and "potentially present[ed] a safety concern." Because "ICE OPR did not have any information about Mr. Streever when the email came in," Goodwin says in an August 5 declaration, it "determined that it needed to conduct an ICE investigation."
What happened next makes little sense if ICE's investigators, who did not even try to contact Streever until five months after his email, were attempting to resolve a legitimate "safety concern." But their actions are completely understandable if they were trying to intimidate an ICE critic.
"YOU MAY BE IN VIOLATION OF FEDERAL LAW," said the "WARNING NOTICE" that two agents left with Streever's wife in Rochester on June 23. It cited two statutes, one dealing with threats of violence against federal officials, the other making it a crime to reveal "restricted personal information" about them with the intent to intimidate or incite violence against them.
Streever had not violated either of those laws. But the notice said ICE had "reason to believe" his email to Lyons "may constitute a violation of Title 18 of the United States Code," which includes more than 1,500 offenses.
The document asked Streever to "promptly remove and/or discontinue the aforementioned behavior." It added that "receipt of this Notice will be taken into consideration, should you continue to be involved in any criminal activities described above."
In addition to delivering the notice, DHS agents unsuccessfully tried to intercept Streever at John F. Kennedy International Airport when he returned from a trip to Finland with his 7-year-old daughter on June 25. They also repeatedly tried to contact him in person and by telephone at the New York hotel where he stayed that night.
After that, Goodwin says, ICE gave up, closing the case on June 30 because "all investigative leads" had been "exhausted." ICE did that even though its agents had never managed to interview Streever so they could determine "whether or not [he] presented a threat," which Goodwin describes as the object of the investigation.
Seeking dismissal of Streever's lawsuit, the government's lawyers concede his email to Lyons "put words to his disagreements with a current administration official." In other words, they admit he was investigated because of speech protected by the First Amendment.
Other ICE critics have received similar treatment. The Wall Street Journal reports that the agency "has deployed a round-the-clock digital dragnet" that tracks online speech to identify more targets.
ICE's retaliatory campaign, Streever's lawyers at the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression warn, threatens the freedom to criticize police conduct without fear of arrest. Four decades ago, the Supreme Court described that ability as "one of the principal characteristics by which we distinguish a free nation from a police state."

articles.title: Minnesota's "Nudification" Ban Repeats Unconstitutional Errors of Early Revenge Porn Bills
articles.content:
十多年前，各州开始制定法律禁止所谓的「报复性色情」行为。一些伴侣之间会自愿交换性爱照片，但在关系结束后，一方可能会出于报复将这些隐私图像公开。后来，「非自愿色情」一词更为普遍，因为这些照片并非总是由前伴侣分享。

早期法律中的许多条款实际上采用了严格责任标准，而没有对认知（scienter）提出任何要求。随着时间的推移，这些法律被修改以包含认知要求，这些限制措施对于通过严格审查至关重要。

尽管我最初对早期「报复性色情」法案的合宪性持怀疑态度，但后来我得出结论，认知要求以及其他限制措施使这些法律得以生存。例如，明尼苏达州最高法院在《州诉卡西利亚斯案》（2020年）中维持了该州的报复性色情法律。该法院观察到：
其次，被告必须「故意」传播图像。明尼苏达州法律§617.261，第1款。这种心理要件意味着被告必须知道并自愿传播私人性爱图像；疏忽、意外甚至鲁莽的传播行为不受禁止。这种特定意图要求进一步缩小了法律范围，避免其「针对广泛的言论类别」。

这一背景有助于解释为什么明尼苏达州的新法律是违宪的。该法律通常被称为人工智能「裸化」禁令，但其范围远超预期。法律部分规定：
第2款。禁止裸化。
（a）任何拥有或控制网站、应用程序、软件、程序或其他服务的人不得：
（1）允许用户通过网站、应用程序、软件、程序或其他服务访问、下载或使用裸化图像或视频；或
（2）代表用户裸化图像或视频。

该法律将「裸化」定义为「图像或视频被更改或生成以显示原始未更改图像或视频中未显示的可识别个人的隐私部位」。唯一的例外是当网站「要求用户具备技术技能才能裸化图像或视频」。该法律缺乏任何认知要求，也没有对具有艺术、政治、医学或其他教育价值的图像设立任何豁免条款。

xAI公司（Grok的制造商）质疑该禁令的合宪性。地区法院拒绝了临时限制令（TRO）并安排听证会。申请初步禁令的程序已完成。

xAI认为（我同意这一观点），该法律缺乏认知要求，因此违宪：
该法案通过省略任何可能将其限制在解决立法机构所描述的危害范围内的限制条款，加剧了这一问题。它没有认知要求，因此责任取决于用户所做的事情，而不是提供者知道或可以预防的事情。它从未提及同意，因此一个编辑自己照片的女性将与一个编辑她照片的陌生人受到同样对待。

明尼苏达州并未直接回应这一论点，而是主张在中度审查标准下，无需认知要求。我认为这一论点站不住脚。该法律是基于内容的，因为它直接根据生成图像的内容触发责任。（这是我在3D打印枪械诉讼中长期以来一直提出的论点。）一张全身穿衣的图像不会导致责任，但一张穿着比基尼的男子照片可能会导致责任。缺乏认知要求意味着该法律缺乏必要的狭窄限制。xAI的公文引用了上述明尼苏达州最高法院的案例。

xAI承认该工具可能被滥用，并提供了Grok已经设立的多项防护措施。初步禁令公文开头写道：
一州在保护其公民免受真实伤害的同时，仍必须尊重这些公民在努力中的基本权利。在制定HF1606时，问题不在于明尼苏达州试图推进禁止未经同意分享真实人物的人工生成裸体图像这一合法利益。xAI并不质疑这一利益，并且严格禁止其用户在未经同意的情况下生成裸体或性化图像。实际上，xAI已经起诉试图绕过其广泛的技术封锁生成此类图像的用户。问题在于HF1606远远超出了立法机构声称的目标范围，影响了宪法同样保护的其他同等重要的权利。

范围过宽的问题是明尼苏达州应该熟悉的。三十多年前，在《R.A.V.诉圣保罗市》案中，最高法院宣告该州另一项善意的法律违反第一修正案。斯卡利亚大法官指出：
让我们不要误解我们对在别人庭院前烧十字架行为的可恶程度有何疑义。但圣保罗有足够的手段可以阻止这种行为，而无需将第一修正案投入火中。

对裸化法律可以作出相同的评论。利用人工智能故意生成真实人物的裸体图像是可恶的。但明尼苏达州有能力制定一项精心设计的法律来实现这一目标。在第一修正案的上下文中，法院审查法律的撰写，而非律师提出的法律。
articles.summary:
More than a decade ago, states began enacting laws to prohibit so-called "revenge porn." Some partners would voluntarily exchange sexual photographs, but after the relationship ended, one of the partners would share the intimate images as a form of revenge. Later, the term "non-consensual pornography" became more common, as the pictures were not always shared by former partners.

Many of the early bills imposed what was effectively a strict liability standard without any scienter requirement. Over time, these bills were modified to include a scienter requirement, and these guardrails were essential to survive strict scrutiny.

While I doubted the constitutionality of early revenge porn bills, I came to the conclusion that the scienter requirement, as well as other guard rails, saved the laws. For example, the Minnesota Supreme Court upheld the state's revenge porn law in light of this narrow tailoring. That court observed in State v. Casillas (2020):

Second, a defendant must "intentionally" disseminate the image. Minn. Stat. § 617.261, subd. 1. This mens rea requirement means that a defendant must knowingly and voluntarily disseminate a private sexual image; negligent, accidental, or even reckless distributions are not proscribed. This specific intent requirement further narrows the statute and keeps it from "target[ing] broad categories of speech." Muccio, 890 N.W.2d at 928.

This background helps explain why a new Minnesota law is unconstitutional. This statute is commonly called an AI "Nudification" Ban, but it sweeps far more broadly. It provides in part:

Subd. 2. Nudification prohibited.

(a) A person who owns or controls a website, application, software, program, or other service must not:

(1) allow a user to access, download, or use the website, application, software, program, or other service to nudify an image or video; or

(2) nudify an image or video on behalf of a user.

The statute defines "nudify," in part, as "an image or video is altered or generated to depict an intimate part not depicted in an original unaltered image or video of an identifiable individual." The only exemption is when the web site "requires the technical skill of a user to nudify an image or video." The statute lacks any scienter requirement. The statute also lacks any exemption for images that have artistic, political, medical, or other educational value.

xAI, the maker of Grok, challenged the constitutionality of the ban. The district court denied the TRO and set the case for a preliminary injunction proceeding. That briefing has now completed.

xAI argues (correctly in my view) that the statute's lack of a scienter requirement renders the law unconstitutional:

The Act then compounds the problem by omitting every limit that might have confined it to addressing the harm the Legislature described. It has no scienter requirement, so liability turns on what a user managed to do rather than on anything the provider knew or could have prevented. It never mentions consent, so a woman who edits a photograph of herself is treated exactly like a stranger who edits her picture.

Minnesota doesn't really engage that argument, but instead contends that under intermediate scrutiny, there is no scienter requirement. I don't think this argument works. This statute is content-based, as it triggers liability directly based on the content of the generated image. (This is an argument I have advanced for some time in the 3D-printed gun litigation.) An image generated with people fully-clothed would not be subject to liability. But a picture of a shirtless man wearing speedos could generate liability. The absence of a scienter requirement, in this case, means the statute lacks the requisite narrow tailing. xAI's brief cites the Minnesota Supreme Court case mentioned above.

xAI recognizes how this tool can be abused, and the brief demonstrates numerous safeguards that Grock has put in place. The PI brief begins:

A state that seeks to guard its citizens against real harms nevertheless must also respect those same citizens' fundamental rights in the effort. In enacting HF 1606, the trouble is not that Minnesota sought to advance a legitimate interest in prohibiting the dissemination of artificially generated nude images of real people without their consent. xAI does not contest that interest, and it strictly prohibits its users from generating nude or sexualized images of people without their consent. Indeed, xAI has filed suit against users who evade its extensive technological blockers to generate such images in violation of this strict prohibition. The problem is that HF 1606 stretches far beyond the Legislature's claimed target to hit other, equally important rights protected by the Constitution.

The problem of overbreadth is something Minnesota should be familiar with. More than three decades ago, in R.A.V. v. City of St. Paul, the Supreme Court declared another well-intentioned law from the Land of 10,000 Lakes as a violation of the First Amendment. Justice Scalia observed:

Let there be no mistake about our belief that burning a cross in someone's front yard is reprehensible. But St. Paul has sufficient means at its disposal to prevent such behavior without adding the First Amendment to the fire.

Much the same can be said about the nudification law. The intentional use of AI for generating nude images of people is reprehensible. but Minnesota has the means to craft a carefully tailored statute to achieve this goal. In the First Amendment context, the court reviews the statute as drafted, and not the statute the lawyers present.

The post Minnesota's "Nudification" Ban Repeats Unconstitutional Errors of Early Revenge Porn Bills appeared first on Reason.com.

articles.title: Voter Ignorance and the Problem of Confusion Caused by Candidates With Similar Names [Updated]
articles.content:
康奈尔大学法学教授迈克尔·多夫在近期一篇有趣的博客中指出，阿拉斯加州目前正在进行的参议院选举中有两位候选人名字几乎相同，其中一人可能是为了从对手那里争取选票而参选的。

在今天的参议院初选中，阿拉斯加州选民将面临许多选择，其中包括两位名为丹·萨利文（Dan Sullivan）的候选人。一位是共和党现任参议员，另一位是阿拉斯加彼得斯堡退休教师，名字相同。共和党人声称，这位退休教师，我暂称其为“教师丹”，参选的唯一或主要目的是通过分流选票来削弱现任参议员，从而可能使民主党挑战者在一场激烈的竞选中获胜。这种指控在丛林初选模式下是合理的。今天初选中排名前四的候选人将进入总统大选。如果这四人中有两人名为丹·萨利文，这可能足以使民主党挑战者、现任众议院议员玛丽·佩尔托拉（Mary Peltola）获胜。

“教师丹”是否仅仅（或主要）为了分流现任丹的选票而参选？纽约时报今天的报道给出了一个不确定的结论。教师丹激烈地否认自己是作为破坏者/分流者参选的，声称希望将共和党从“让美国再次伟大”转向传统的规范和立场。然而，同一报道也指出，通过活动和捐款表达的教师丹的观点相当主流自由民主党派……

这两个名字并非完全相同。现任参议员是丹·S·萨利文（Dan S. Sullivan），“教师丹”（多夫如此称呼他）是丹·J·萨利文（Dan J. Sullivan）。但相似之处很大。

多夫指出，如果“教师丹”的竞选成功利用了选民对两人名字的混淆，这显然在某种程度上削弱了有效的选民选择。我同意，尽管——就像多夫一样——我最终更希望民主党候选人玛丽·佩尔托拉赢得这场竞选，因为她的立场比目前特朗普主导的共和党中大多数候选人的立场要好得多。

多夫还指出，这并非第一次选民可能因候选人名字相似而感到困惑。除了他提到的案例外，还有2003年加州州长召回选举的例子，当时一位名叫乔治·施瓦茨曼（George Schwartzman）的不为人知的候选人在135位候选人中排名第九，击败了几位更知名的候选人，很可能是因为选民混淆了他和著名演员阿诺德·施瓦辛格（Arnold Schwarzenegger）的名字。施瓦辛格仍然轻松获胜。但在一场接近的选举中，施瓦茨曼得到的近11,000张选票可能会起决定性作用。

多夫指出，如果“教师丹”确实主要是通过混淆来分流选票，那么他的行为是否合法尚不清楚。虽然利用混淆是道德上的可恶行为，但我不确定是否应该起诉采取这种行为的候选人。他们确实在试图欺骗选民。但许多其他候选人也经常就各种问题撒谎和歪曲事实。

唐纳德·特朗普是一个特别恶劣的例子，从他2016年的第一次竞选开始，最近又在2020年大选和其他问题上撒谎。但更传统的政治家也经常诉诸谎言和欺骗，尽管程度不如特朗普。例如，奥巴马总统在谈到《可负担医疗保险法》时，著名地撒谎称“如果你喜欢你的医疗保险计划，你可以保持它”。这种欺骗赢得了2013年Politifact年度谎言奖。但它仍然帮助奥巴马在2012年连任。我不确定利用选民对名字的混淆是否比利用他们对政策问题（如犯罪、移民和医疗保健）的无知更糟。

试图通过刑事和民事责任来防止这种利用可能会违反第一修正案。此外，这可能会给现任政治领导人广泛的权力来限制言论和控制选举竞争，而这种权力他们不能被信任。

最终，利用选民对名字的混淆和其他竞选中的欺骗都是为了利用普遍的选民无知。由于“理性无知”（缺乏寻求政治信息的激励）和“理性非理性”（缺乏进行无偏评估的激励）的结合，大多数选民对政府和公共政策知之甚少，并且经常做出不良的信息评估。这使他们容易受到欺骗和操纵，并激励政治家撒谎和歪曲真相。

选民对名字相似的候选人感到困惑只是这个更广泛的问题的另一个例子。密切关注政治并仔细阅读选票的选民不太可能区分不清两位丹·萨利文。实际上，由于这件事在媒体上的广泛报道，他们可能会提前了解到这个问题，并在投票时注意到这一点。施瓦辛格和施瓦茨曼之间的区别也一样。但由于投票的激励结构，大多数人不太关注，也不太仔细填写选票。因此，许多人可能会被名字相似的候选人混淆。

选民无知的问题没有简单的解决方案。但在我的2023年文章《解决政治无知的自上而下和自下而上的方案》和之前的著作《民主与政治无知》中，我评估了一系列可能的选项。我认为最好的方法是减少通过选票进行的决策，增加通过“用脚投票”的决策，因为后者寻求信息和智慧评估的激励更好。但我认识到，任何有效的方法都需要时间，可能没有单一的解决方案足够。我们可能需要追求多种策略。在此期间，选民可能会继续对各种问题感到无知和困惑，政治家和利益集团也可能继续利用这一点。

更新：我对这篇文章进行了小幅补充。

更新#2：在选举法律博客上，著名选举法律学者里克·哈森指出，司法部正在调查丹·J·萨利文，并认为在这种情况下提起起诉将面临严重的第一修正案问题，并可能违宪：

如果J最终被指控违反了《美利坚合众国诉美国白人至上主义协会》（18 U.S.C. s 241），该法惩罚“任何州内的任何人通过阴谋‘伤害、压迫、威胁或恐吓任何人’……在行使或享受宪法或合众国法律赋予其的任何权利或特权方面”，我认为J将有一个非常强有力的第一修正案辩护（对电信诈骗指控可能也是如此，但我不确定指控的基础是什么）……

[T]这不是关于欺骗某人关于选举机制以不投票的案件。这也不是关于冒充的案件：J确实名为“Daniel Sullivan”。甚至不是案件J说谎……

这是关于一个人出于不纯的动机参选，并恰好有一个可以混淆一些选民的名字……

我不明白政府如何能够将其参选行为定为犯罪。如果可以这样做，那么每次共和党支持绿党候选人，或者民主党支持初选中的MAGA候选人，希望该候选人在总统大选中对民主党候选人更弱，都可能构成犯罪。这种情况经常发生。

让国家开始对人们的政治信仰和秘密动机进行刑事起诉是非常危险的。我们要举行审判，并探查人们的政治立场吗？

我基本同意哈森在这一点上的分析。“教师丹”的行为可能可鄙，就像许多利用选民无知撒谎和欺骗的政治家一样。但它可能无法被起诉。
articles.summary:
As Cornell law Professor Michael Dorf explains in an interesting recent blog post, the currently ongoing Senate election in Alaska includes two candidates with almost identical names, one of whom may well be in the race to siphon off votes from the other:

In today's Senate primary election, Alaska voters will have many choices, including two named Dan Sullivan. One is the incumbent Republican. The other is a retired schoolteacher from Petersburg, Alaska with the same name. Republicans claim that the man I'll call Teacher Dan is running for the sole (or at least main) purpose of siphoning votes off from the incumbent and thus potentially handing victory to the Democratic challenger in a tight race. That's a plausible allegation given the jungle primary format. The top four finishers in today's primary advance to the general election. If two of those candidates are named Dan Sullivan, that could be enough to tip the outcome in favor of Democratic challenger and current House member Mary Peltola.

Is Teacher Dan in it only (or mostly) to siphon votes from Incumbent Dan? A NY Times story today reaches an uncertain verdict. Teacher Dan vociferously denies that he's running as a spoiler/siphoner, professing a desire to turn the Republican Party away from MAGAism and back towards its traditional norms and positions. However, the same story also indicates that Teacher Dan's views, as expressed through activism and donations, are pretty mainstream liberal Democratic….

The names are not quite completely identical. The incumbent senator is Dan S. Sullivan, and "Teacher Dan" (as Dorf calls him) is Dan J. Sullivan. But the similarity is great.

As Dorf notes, if "Teacher Dan's" campaign succeeds in exploiting voter confusion about the two men's names, there is an obvious sense in which it is undermining effective voter choice. I agree, even though - like Dorf - I would ultimately prefer that Democrat Mary Peltola win this race, as her positions are much less bad than those of most Republicans in the current Trump-dominated version of the GOP.

As Dorf notes, this is far from the first time that voters may get confused by candidates with similar names. In addition to cases he indicates, there is the example of the 2003 California gubernatorial recall election, where little-known candidate George Schwartzman finished ninth out of 135 candidates, beating several better-known ones, likely because voters were confused by the fact that his name is similar to that of famous actor Arnold Schwarzenegger. Schwarzenegger still won easily. But in a close election, the nearly 11,000 votes that Schwartzman got might have proved decisive.

Dorf points out that if "Teacher Dan" really is in the race primarily to siphon off votes through confusion, it is not clear whether his actions are illegal. While such exploitation of confusion is morally reprehensible, I am not sure it is a good idea to prosecute candidates who do this. They are indeed trying to deceive voters. But the same is true of many other candidates who routinely lie about and distort  issues of all kinds.

Donald Trump is a particularly egregious example, going all the way back to his first campaign in 2016, and more recently with his lies about the 2020 election and other issues. But more conventional politicians also often resort to lies and deception, even if not to the same degree.  President Obama, for example, famously  lied when he claimed that, under the Affordable Care Act, "if you like your health care plan, you can keep it." That deception won the 2013 Politifact Lie of the Year award. But it still helped Obama get reelected in 2012. I am not sure exploiting voter confusion about names is any worse than exploiting their ignorance about policy issues like crime, immigration, and health care.

Trying to prevent such exploitation through criminal and civil liability is likely to violate the First Amendment. In addition, it would likely end up giving incumbent political leaders broad power to curb speech and control electoral campaigns that they cannot be trusted with.

Ultimately, both exploitation of voter confusion about names and other deceptions used in campaigns seek to exploit widespread voter ignorance. Because of the combination of "rational ignorance" (lack of incentive to seek out political information) and "rational irrationality" (lack of incentive to engage in unbiased evaluation),  most voters know little about government and public policy, and often do a poor job of evaluating the information they do know. This makes them vulnerable to deception and manipulation, and incentivizes politicians to lie and otherwise distort the truth.

Voter confusion about candidates with similar names is just another example of this broader problem. Voters who follow politics closely and pay careful attention to their ballots should have little trouble distinguishing between the two Dan Sullivans. Indeed, they would likely know about this issue ahead of time thanks to all the media coverage it has gotten, and would thereby watch out for it when at the polls. The same goes for the difference between Schwarzenegger and Schwartzman, and other such situations. But, due to the incentive structure of voting, most people do not pay such close attention and are not especially careful in filling out ballots. Thus, many might be confused by candidates with similar names.

There is no easy solution to the problem of voter ignorance. But I assess a range of possible options in my 2023 article on "Top-Down and Bottom-Up Solutions to the Problem of Political Ignorance, and in my earlier book Democracy and Political Ignorance. I believe the best approach is to make fewer decisions at the ballot box and more by "voting with your feet," where incentives to seek out information and evaluate it wisely are much better. But I  recognize that any effective approach will take time, and there may be no one fix that is sufficient by itself.  We may need to pursue multiple strategies. In the meantime, voters are likely to continue to be ignorant and confused about a variety of issues, and politicians and interest groups are likely to keep on exploiting that.

UPDATE: I have made minor additions to this post.

UPDATE #2: At the Election Law Blog, prominent election law scholar Rick Hasen notes that the Justice Department is investigating Dan J. Sullivan, and argues that an prosecution here would raise serious First Amendment concerns, and likely be unconstitutional:

If J. ultimately is charged with violating the Ku Klux Klan Act (18 U.S.C. s 241), which punishes a conspiracy to "injure, oppress, threaten, or intimidate any person in any State. . . in the free exercise or enjoyment of any right or privilege secured to him by the Constitution or laws of the United States," I think J. would have a very strong First Amendment defense (and likely for the wire fraud claims too, but I don't know enough about what the basis for those charges might be)….

[T]his is not a case about tricking someone about the mechanics of the election not to vote. Nor is it a case of impersonation: J. is really named "Daniel Sullivan." It is not even a case about J. telling a campaign lie….

This is a case about someone running for office with impure motives who is lucky enough to have a name that could confuse some voters….

I don't see how the government could criminalize his running for office for having impure motives. And if it could do so, then it could be a crime every time that the Republican Party backs a Green Party candidate, or Democrats support a MAGA candidate in a primary in the hopes that the candidate would be weaker against a Democrat in the general election. This stuff happens all the time.

It would be quite dangerous for the state to start criminally prosecuting people for their political beliefs and secret motives. Are we going to put people on trial and probe their political allegiances?

I largely agree with Hasen's analysis on this point. "Teacher Dan's" behavior may be reprehensible, as is that of many politicians who use lies and deception exploit voter ignorance. But it probably cannot be prosecuted.

The post Voter Ignorance and the Problem of Confusion Caused by Candidates With Similar Names [Updated] appeared first on Reason.com.

articles.title: The Greater the Illegal Migrant Population, the Stronger the Case Against Mass Deportation
articles.content:
美国非法移民人口的标准估计在1100万到1500万之间。但右翼限制移民派经常声称实际数字远高于此，比如特朗普曾宣称有2.5亿非法移民。他们的潜台词是人口越多，大规模驱逐的理由越充分。但卡托研究所的移民政策专家大卫·比尔在最近的文章中（全文需付费）指出，事实恰恰相反：

数学很简单。非法移民越多，强制遣返的成本就越高。国土安全部估计，单次驱逐的平均成本为18245美元。这意味着当特朗普虚构出1000万额外非法移民时，理论上就为驱逐开支增加了1824亿美元。

而这仅是驱逐成本。对联邦财政的影响更为显著。非法移民支付销售税、社会保障税、所得税和财产税。驱逐越多非法移民，政府财政负担就越多转移到美国公民和合法居民身上。国会预算办公室估计，近期到来的非法移民将在10年内使财政赤字减少近1万亿美元，而特朗普2025年的强硬政策已消耗其中5000亿美元的收益。

非法移民获得的纳税人福利极少，因为他们无资格享受所有最大的联邦公共福利项目，多数州也限制了对较小规模州项目的资格。由于福利支付是已知量，更大的非法移民群体意味着每人成本实际上远低于我们想象的。

但纳税人开支与更广泛的经济影响相比微不足道：为美国人生产的产品减少。彼得森国际经济研究所估计，仅830万的驱逐将使2028年的美国国内生产总值比原本水平低7.4%，相当于约2.5万亿美元。产出降低意味着货物和服务减少——从食品到儿童保育等一切对美国人而言。

更高的非法移民数字还意味着他们犯罪率比传统估计更低（传统估计已显示其犯罪率远低于美国本土出生人士）：

如果特朗普政府夸大的数字属实，将意味着非法移民的犯罪率比我们想象的更低。使用远低于此的非法移民数字，学者们已计算出，与本土美国人相比，非法移民被监禁的可能性较低。但由于我们已知监狱在押人员身份，如果自由移民群体增长，移民监禁率也会随之下降。

换句话说，特朗普政府显然认为非法移民在犯罪数据中存在程度远高于其他人群的低代表性。当然，重要的是犯罪率而非绝对犯罪数字，因为率反映了人们成为犯罪受害者的可能性。更多移民意味着更低的受害率——非法移民的存在降低了美国人遭受犯罪的可能性。

我还要补充，驱逐更多非法移民（或尝试驱逐）会加剧驱逐行动对美国公民公民权利的严重影响，包括种族歧视、非法拘留、伤害和杀害抗议者等。

此外，驱逐更多民众会增加将许多人驱赶回终身贫困和压迫、甚至早逝的风险。仅因出生于错误的家庭或地区而强迫改变命运是不公正的。

正如大卫·比尔指出，尽管非法移民的犯罪率低于美国公民，但仍有少数人犯罪。解决方法很简单：和其他人一样惩罚他们！我在其他文章中（如这里和这里）解释过，我们可以通过取消移民与海关执法局（ICE）并将其资源转移至普通警方来显著降低整体犯罪率，后者专注打击暴力和财产犯罪。

结束或至少限制驱逐行动还能进一步降低犯罪率，因为这将使西班牙裔犯罪受害者更愿意向警方报案。当地方和州警方协助联邦驱逐行动时，报案率下降，从而显著增加犯罪。由于移民执法机构普遍存在种族偏见，即使合法西班牙裔也常恐惧与执法者互动，若后者参与驱逐行动。显然，许多公民和合法移民有未经登记的亲属，或因特朗普政府大规模剥夺许多移民的合法身份而成为非法移民，包括逃离共产主义的古巴、尼加拉瓜和委内瑞拉人，逃离激进伊斯兰主义的伊朗基督徒，逃离西半球最贫穷、最暴力社会之一的海地人等。

总之，非法移民人数越多，反对大规模驱逐的理由越充分。
articles.summary:
Standard estimates of the illegal/undocumented immigrant population in the United States range from about 11 million to 15 million. But right-wing immigration restrictionists often assert the true figure is much higher, as with Donald Trump's  claim that it is 25 million. The implicit assumption is that the higher the number, the stronger the case for mass deportation. But, as my Cato Institute colleague David Bier - a leading immigration policy expert - explains in a recent article (fuller, but paywalled version here) the exact opposite is true:

The math is simple. The more illegal immigrants, the more Americans would have to pay to deport them. The Department of Homeland Security estimates that a single deportation costs on average $18,245. This means that when Trump invents the presence of 10 million more immigrants, he's adding a theoretical $182.4 billion to the price tag.

And that's just the cost of deportation. The cost to federal revenue is even starker. Illegal immigrants pay sales tax — and, often, Social Security tax, income tax and property tax. The more illegal immigrants we deport, the more the cost of funding government would shift to American citizens and legal residents. The Congressional Budget Office estimated that recent illegal immigrant arrivals would have cut deficits by nearly $1 trillion over 10 years, and  found that Trump's crackdown in 2025 had already erased $500 billion of those savings.

Illegal immigrants receive very few taxpayer benefits because they are ineligible for all the largest federal public benefit programs, and most states also restrict eligibility for smaller state programs. Since the benefits being paid are a known quantity, a larger illegal immigrant population suggests that the cost per immigrant is actually far lower than we think.

But the taxpayer expenses are dwarfed by the broader economic impact: less stuff produced for the American people. The Peterson Institute for International Economics has estimated that just 8.3 million deportations would leave U.S. gross domestic product 7.4% lower than otherwise by 2028, the equivalent of about $2.5 trillion. Lower output means fewer goods and services — everything from food to childcare — for Americans.

Higher figures also imply that the illegal migrants have an even lower crime rate than under conventional estimates of their numbers (which already show them to commit crimes at a much lower rate than native-born Americans):

If the Trump administration's hyperinflated figures were true, it would also suggest that illegal immigrants commit crimes at much lower rates than we thought. Using a far lower estimate of the number of illegal immigrants in the country, scholars had already calculated that, compared to native-born Americans, illegal immigrants  were far less likely to be incarcerated. But again, since we know who is in prison, if the free immigrant population were to grow, the immigrant incarceration rate would fall in turn.

In other words, the Trump administration apparently believes that illegal immigrants are far less represented in the crime data than anyone else. Of course, the rate of crime — not the absolute number of crimes — is what matters, because the rate is how we estimate the likelihood that someone will become a victim of a crime. More immigrants would mean a much lower victimization rate — that the presence of illegal immigrants reduces the likelihood that Americans will be victimized.

I would add that deporting larger numbers of illegal migrants (or even trying to do so) increases the already severe impact of deportation efforts on the civil liberties of US citizens, including through racial profiling, illegal detention, killing and injuring of protestors, and more.

Furthermore, deporting larger numbers of people increases the number sent back to what for many is a lifetime of poverty and oppression, and sometimes an early death. It is unjust to use force to consign people to such a fate merely because they were born to the wrong parents in the wrong place.

As David Bier notes, some illegal migrants nonetheless do commit crimes, even if at a lower rate than US citizens. The answer to that problem is simple: just punish them the same as anyone else! As I have explained in other writings (e.g. here and here), we can significantly reduce crime rates, overall simply by abolishing ICE and transferring its resources to ordinary police, tasked with fighting violent and property crime.

Ending, or at least curbing, deportation operations would further lower crime by making Hispanic crime victims more willing to report crimes to the police. When local and state police assist in federal deportation efforts, reporting drops, thereby increasing crime significantly. Given widespread racial profiling by immigration enforcement agencies, even legally present Hispanics may often fear interactions with law enforcement, if the latter are involved in deportation efforts. And, obviously, many citizens and legal migrants have relatives who are undocumented, or who have been rendered so by the Trump Administration's massive effort to strip legal status from many immigrants who had it before, including Cubans, Nicaraguans and Venezuelans who fled communism, Iranian Christians who fled radical Islamism, Haitians who fled one of the Western Hemisphere's poorest and most violent societies, and more.

In sum, the greater the number of illegal migrants, the stronger the case against mass deportation.

The post The Greater the Illegal Migrant Population, the Stronger the Case Against Mass Deportation appeared first on Reason.com.

articles.title: Ibram X. Kendi Is Wrong About Jason Arday
articles.content:
剑桥大学知名黑人教授贾森·阿戴（Jason Arday）因涉嫌严重抄袭而辞职，不久后去世，引发争议。他的支持者指责媒体种族主义，但他本人的学术不端和个人欺骗行为也是关键因素。

伦敦市长萨迪克·汗（Sadiq Khan）批评媒体对阿戴进行“恶毒的公开羞辱”，反种族主义组织“反对种族主义联盟”则表示阿戴遭受了种族主义“巫师猎人”的迫害。美国著名反种族主义学者伊布拉姆·肯迪（Ibram X. Kendi）更是直言：“媒体是对阿戴进行了‘林奇式审判’。”

肯迪在社交媒体上写道：“作为一名知名的反种族主义黑人学者，你永远是被围攻的目标，随时可能遭受如‘林奇暴徒’般的攻击。而当你因这些攻击而死亡时，媒体仍会将这些攻击称作‘指控’，试图洗清自己的罪责。这种说法完全荒谬且令人深恶痛绝。”

然而，阿戴的学术和个人问题并非无中生有。他曾在个人背景上大肆编造，包括声称自己患有严重自闭症、11岁前无法言语、跑过600英里、筹集巨额慈善金等。这些明显不符合常理的说法早已引起广泛关注。此外，他的学术工作粗糙，多次涉嫌抄袭。

阿戴在剑桥大学地位显赫，甚至曾为英国政府的教育课程提供建议。当《泰晤士高等教育》记者杰克·格罗夫（Jack Grove）对他的工作和背景提出质疑时，阿戴非但没有正面回应，反而报警，要求警方调查格罗夫。警方随即告知格罗夫不要再联系阿戴，因为这会影响他的心理健康。

阿戴的死亡确实是悲剧，但他的问题完全是自找的。他试图用警察来威慑批评者，这种行为与学术自由和自由探讨的原则格格不入。然而，一些人却反其道而行之，要求限制言论和新闻自由，以防止对弱势群体造成情感伤害。

作家兼记者马特·哈伊格（Matt Haig）呼吁英国首相安迪·伯纳姆（Andy Burnham）采取行动，惩罚那些针对弱势群体实施政治攻击的记者。他写道：“英国记者可以毫无后果地针对弱势群体发动政治攻势，这严重损害了英国的道德形象。”这种言论实际上是对审查的支持，是错误的。不能滥用心理健康概念来否决合理的批评。

阿戴的死是悲剧，但我们不能因此指责那些揭露他荒谬谎言的人。如果我们开始限制对公众人物的合理质疑，包括知名学者，那么重要的机构，如学术界，将免受批评，这是一个严重的错误。高等教育正面临合法性危机，部分原因是被认为由脱离现实的自由派精英利用种族和意识形态取代了能力，允许江湖术士推销无法经得起考验的研究。在美国，这种情况已经引发强烈反弹，特朗普政府也采取了多项措施削弱多元性、公平性和包容性（DEI）计划。

如果我们希望精英文化更加封闭，更容易被坏人操控，那么阿戴的支持者的劝告会是一个明智的选择：他们想要将质疑阿戴的行为定为犯罪。这种做法只会加剧学术界的问题，而非解决问题。
articles.summary:
Are the media responsible for the demise of a famous black professor at the University of Cambridge? Jason Arday was found dead last week after resigning from the university following widespread serious plagiarism allegations. But his defenders say Arday was unfairly targeted by racist reactionaries. Sadiq Khan, the mayor of London, assailed the media for engaging in a campaign of "pernicious public shaming," and the activist group Stand Up to Racism said he'd been subjected to a racist witch hunt.

Most notably, the anti-racist activist Ibram X. Kendi stated unequivocally that "the media lynched Jason Arday."

The death of Jason Arday hit so close to home that I had no words yesterday. But I woke up with words.

To be a prominent antiracist Black scholar is to know you are a target, almost totally surrounded by resentments. You know that at any point, the attacks can come like a lynch… pic.twitter.com/XetSepzJrx

— Ibram X. Kendi (@ibramxk) August 15, 2026

He writes:

To be a prominent antiracist Black scholar is to know you are a target, almost totally surrounded by resentments. You know that at any point, the attacks can come like a lynch mob.

And if you die from all the attacks, the media still calls the attacks on you "accusations" to wash their hands of the blood. Your lynchers announce your death as if they had no role in your lynching.

That is completely and utterly absurd. It's grossly offensive. And it elides the real harms that Arday perpetrated: serial plagiarism, fabulism, and lying. Now, Arday's death is clearly a tragedy, and no one should be making light of it. There's nothing good or pleasant about this sad affair. But when Kendi and others accuse the media of complicity in his death, what they are essentially saying is that it's your fault for noticing and calling out his serious transgressions—that he should have been left alone to continue lying about who he was and his qualifications.

And to be clear, the fact that Arday was a fabulist is not in dispute at all. He made outrageous and self-discrediting claims about his background: alleged crippling autism, being nonverbal until age 11, running 600 miles, raising huge sums of money for charity. Those were widely noted details of his personal life, and he simply lied about them. And that's without even getting into his professional failings: his sloppy work, his continuous plagiarism.

It's not as if he was some harmless or vaguely relevant academic. He was a huge deal at Cambridge, and even advised the British government on the school's curriculum. And when a reporter for Times Higher Education had questions about Arday's work and background, Arday had him investigated by the police. That's right, rather than face well-justified criticism, Arday called the British police on Jack Grove, a journalist. The police told Grove not to contact Arday again because it was negatively impacting his mental health.

And indeed, it probably was. But there's no way around this: Arday brought this on himself by lying.

Moreover, his inclination to sic the cops on a critic was very, very bad behavior and entirely contrary to basic principles of free inquiry—principles that supposedly undergird higher education. Unfortunately, some people are taking the opposite lesson and calling for more restrictions on freedom of speech and press freedoms in order to prevent them from causing emotional harm. The author and journalist Matt Haig called on U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham to take action to punish journalists for engaging in speech. He writes: "The ability right now for UK journalists to face zero consequences for politically motivated campaigns against vulnerable individuals, often in minority groups, is a massive blight on the UK's moral standing."

That right there is an endorsement of censorship, and it's wrong. It's wrong to weaponize the concept of mental health and use it as some kind of veto over legitimate criticism. Arday's death is tragic, and everyone should wish he'd gotten whatever help he needed. But that doesn't mean we should blame the people who called out his sensational lies—and we certainly shouldn't have prevented them from speaking out.

If we start policing people for asking totally legitimate questions of public figures, like a notable academic, then we are quickly going to render important institutions—like academia—immune to criticism. That would be a terrible mistake, quite obviously. Already, higher education is facing a crisis of legitimacy due to the perception—and in some cases, the reality—that out-of-touch liberal elites have used race and ideology as stand-ins for merit, allowing charlatans to peddle dubious research that they can't defend when challenged. Worse, higher education administrators have weaponized the concept of diversity and used it as a cudgel to promote groupthink on cultural issues. In America at least, this has engendered a significant backlash, and the Trump administration has undertaken various efforts to roll back DEI initiatives.

If you want an elite culture that is even more closed-minded, and thus even more prone to capture by bad actors, then you'd do exactly as Arday's defenders are advising: You would make it a crime to call him out.
